intro: Twenty nine verses, and the superscription names no author, only a condition: a prayer for whoever is faint and pouring out his complaint. That is why the psalm has no fixed occasion. It fits any of them. The vocabulary is the vocabulary of a body giving out, bones, heart, skin, sleep, bread and drink, and almost every noun in the first half carries a first person suffix. Then verse 13 says but You, and the psalm changes subject to Zion and to the age of the world without ever resolving the illness it started with.

stichs.en: A prayer of the afflicted, when he grows faint
and pours out his complaint before the LORD.

verses.summary: The heading describes a state rather than a person or an event, which is what makes the psalm reusable by anyone in that state.

stichs.en: LORD, hear my prayer,
and let my cry come to You.

verses.summary: Two requests, and the second one asks less: not that the cry be answered, only that it arrive. Distance is the problem before illness is.

stichs.en: Do not hide Your face from me
on the day I am in distress;
incline Your ear to me;
on the day I call, answer me quickly.

verses.summary: Face and ear, the two organs of attention, one asked not to turn away and one asked to lean in. The word for day repeats and sets a deadline on the answer.

stichs.en: For my days are consumed in smoke,
and my bones are scorched like a hearth.

verses.summary: The complaint proper starts, and it starts with time rather than with pain. Days burn off as smoke, bones burn in place, and the same fire does both.

stichs.en: My heart is struck like grass and has dried up,
for I have forgotten to eat my bread.

verses.summary: Grass enters here and will come back in verse 12 to close the lament. The evidence given for a dried heart is domestic and exact: meals no longer happen.

stichs.en: From the sound of my groaning
my bone clings to my flesh.

verses.summary: Cause and effect run the wrong way round: the noise of grief is what wastes the body, as though the sound itself were doing the work.

stichs.en: I am like a pelican of the wilderness;
I have become like an owl of the ruins.

verses.summary: Two birds, both defined by where they live rather than by what they are. The complaint moves from a failing body to a wrong address.

stichs.en: I lie awake, and I have become
like a bird alone on a roof.

verses.summary: The third bird, and the only one on a human building. Sleeplessness puts the speaker above the house he belongs to rather than inside it.

stichs.en: All the day my enemies taunt me;
those who rave against me swear by me.

verses.summary: To swear by someone is to use his fate as the measure of a curse. The speaker has become a byword, which is a social death running alongside the physical one.

stichs.en: For I have eaten ashes like bread,
and mixed my drink with weeping,

verses.summary: Bread returns from verse 5, now replaced by the ash of mourning. Both halves take a normal meal and substitute a mourning rite for one of its parts.

stichs.en: because of Your fury and Your wrath,
for You lifted me up and cast me away.

verses.summary: The cause is named for the first time and it is God, not illness and not enemies. This is the low point of the psalm and the last verse of the first person before the turn.

stichs.en: My days are like a lengthening shadow,
and I dry up like grass.

verses.summary: Grass closes the lament that it opened in verse 5, and the shadow lengthens because the sun is going down. Both images are ways of saying the end is near without saying it.

stichs.en: But You, LORD, are enthroned forever,
and Your renown for generation after generation.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm, two words wide: but You. The same verb that seated the speaker's days on a slope seats God on a throne with no term.

stichs.en: You will rise and have mercy on Zion,
for it is time to favour her,
for the appointed time has come.

verses.summary: The subject shifts from a sick man to a ruined city, and the tense shifts with it from complaint to certainty. The reason given is that a scheduled hour has arrived.

stichs.en: For Your servants take delight in her stones,
and cherish her dust.

verses.summary: The proof that the hour has come is affection for rubble. Stones and dust are what is left of a building, and loving them is treated as evidence rather than as sentiment.

stichs.en: And the nations will fear the name of the LORD,
and all the kings of the earth Your glory.

verses.summary: The second half of the line drops its verb and borrows the one before it, a compression the psalms use constantly. The audience widens from servants to kings.

stichs.en: For the LORD has built Zion,
He has appeared in His glory.

verses.summary: The rebuilding is stated as accomplished, in the middle of a psalm whose speaker is still dying. The future is described in the past tense because it is certain, not because it has happened.

stichs.en: He has turned to the prayer of the destitute,
and has not despised their prayer.

verses.summary: The private prayer of verse 2 comes back as a category, and in the plural. The one voice has been enrolled among everyone else who prays from nothing.

stichs.en: Let this be written for a later generation,
and a people yet to be created will praise Yah.

verses.summary: The psalm asks to be written down, which is the moment it stops being one man's complaint and becomes a text kept for readers who do not exist yet.

stichs.en: For He looked down from the height of His holiness;
from heaven the LORD gazed to earth,

verses.summary: Two verbs of looking, both of them deliberate rather than incidental. The direction is the reverse of the psalm's opening, where the speaker was trying to send a cry upward.

stichs.en: to hear the groaning of the prisoner,
to set free the children of death.

verses.summary: The purpose of the looking, and it lands on exactly the speaker's own case: someone groaning, someone under sentence. He is answered without being named.

stichs.en: so that the name of the LORD may be told in Zion,
and His praise in Jerusalem,

verses.summary: Release is not the end of the chain. The freed prisoner exists in order to say something, which is how the psalm justifies its own survival as a text.

stichs.en: when peoples gather together,
and kingdoms, to serve the LORD.

verses.summary: The widest point of the psalm, and the last line before it collapses back to one man. Nations assemble in Jerusalem and the next verse is about a shortened life.

stichs.en: He has broken my strength on the way;
He has shortened my days.

verses.summary: The return to complaint is abrupt and unexplained, which is the honest part of the psalm: the vision of a rebuilt city has not cured the man who saw it.

stichs.en: I say: my God,
do not take me away in the middle of my days,
You whose years run through all generations.

verses.summary: The one direct petition in the second half, and it is about timing rather than healing. The request is immediately set against the lifespan that has no half.

stichs.en: Long ago You founded the earth,
and the heavens are the work of Your hands.

verses.summary: The answer to a short life is not a longer life but a longer frame. Creation is brought in as the oldest thing available for comparison.

stichs.en: They will perish, but You will stand;
all of them will wear out like a garment;
You will change them like clothing and they will pass away.

verses.summary: Heaven and earth are put on the same schedule as the speaker's body, only slower. The consolation is strange: nothing lasts, so his not lasting is not a punishment.

stichs.en: But You are He,
and Your years will not end.

verses.summary: Two words with no predicate between them, the shortest sentence in the psalm. After a poem full of failing nouns, the one stable thing is stated without describing it.

stichs.en: The children of Your servants will dwell,
and their seed will be established before You.

verses.summary: The psalm ends without healing the man who spoke it. What continues is the line after him, and dwelling is the word it chooses, the settled opposite of a bird on a roof.

pardes.body: Three panels. Verses 2 to 12 are a body giving out, measured throughout in days rather than in symptoms. Verses 13 to 23 leave the body completely and speak of Zion rebuilt and the nations assembling, in a future stated as though already done. Verses 24 to 29 drop back to the speaker, who asks not to be taken in the middle of his life and is answered with the age of the world. The hinge is {{13.0}}, but You, and everything after it runs on the contrast between a lifespan and a throne. Watch the word for my days: it appears in verses 4, 12, 24 and 25, and it marks every seam in the poem.

The birds of verse 7 are traditionally rendered pelican and owl and the identifications are disputed; what the two words carry for certain is habitat rather than species, one fixed to wilderness and one to ruins, which is the whole point of the comparison. {{11.4}} sharpens the complaint by the order of its verbs: You lifted me up and then threw me down, so the height was part of the fall. {{19.5}} uses the verb of Genesis for a people not yet created, which turns the line from a prediction into a promise. And {{25.3}} literally says do not bring me up, understood as do not take me away, one of the several ways the language declines to name death directly.

{{18.3}} is a rare word for the stripped and destitute, and the same root is used elsewhere in the Bible for a bare plant in the desert; the traditional reading holds both senses at once, a man with nothing and a shrub with no water, which matches the birds of verse 7. On {{19.5}}, one reading takes the people yet to be created to be a generation remade by repentance, on the argument that a people already in existence does not need creating. Verse 19 is also where the psalm becomes aware of itself: it asks to be written for a generation not yet born, and that request is the reason a single sick man's complaint was kept as a public text rather than as a private one.

Verse 27 supplies the image the mystical readings work with: worlds wear out like a garment and are exchanged, and the one who changes them is not changed by the change. {{27.7}} is clothing, and clothing in this register is what a thing shows rather than what it is, so a world that ages is a covering that has served its term. {{28.1}} then says only You are He, two words with nothing predicated of them, treated as the point where description has to stop. The ending fits that reading: the speaker is not healed, and what endures is the line of servants after him, continuity taking the place of cure.
